title: How to defend your sites from AI bots — David Mytton, Arcjet
talk_summary: A security talk on defending public websites from AI crawlers and scrapers, covering layered bot detection: robots.txt, user-agent checks, reverse-DNS IP verification, IP reputation, proof-of-work, HTTP signatures, TLS/HTTP fingerprints, and fingerprint-keyed rate limits. It is about protecting inbound web traffic, not about running agent systems internally.

takeaways.technique: Fingerprint-keyed rate limiting instead of IP-keyed
takeaways.what_they_do: Rate limit on a stable client fingerprint (TLS JA3 hash or session ID) rather than IP, since crawlers rotate through large IP pools.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You can't just rate limit on an IP address ... for malicious crawlers, they can just change them themselves.
takeaways.numbers: crawlers using banks of tens or hundreds of thousands of different IP addresses

takeaways.technique: Verify claimed crawler identity via reverse DNS
takeaways.what_they_do: Combine User-Agent string with reverse-DNS lookup against the claimed provider to confirm the source IP really belongs to that crawler.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can look at the source IP address and you can query those services using a reverse DNS lookup

takeaways.technique: Block data-center IPs on human-only endpoints
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat requests from data-center/VPN/proxy IP ranges as suspicious on endpoints meant only for humans (e.g. signup forms).
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have a sign-up form that you're expecting only humans to submit, then it's unlikely that a request that's coming from a data center IP address
takeaways.numbers: 12% of all bot traffic that hit the Cloudflare network was from the AWS network

takeaways.what_they_do: Front the app with a proof-of-work proxy (Anubis, Nepenthes) that makes suspicious clients spend CPU before access, cheap for one human but expensive at crawler scale.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you have a crawler that's going to tens of thousands or millions of websites and it's having to solve this puzzle every single time, it becomes very expensive

takeaways.technique: robots.txt as a starting signal, not a defense
takeaways.what_they_do: Use robots.txt to declare intent for good bots, but assume bad bots ignore it and may even use disallow rules to find juicy pages.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they're actually using this to find pages on your site that you've disallowed other bots to go to and deliberately going out and getting that content
takeaways.numbers: Read the Docs cut bandwidth from 800 GB/day to 200 GB/day by blocking AI crawlers
